d1637e23-6566-5e45-af4c-b27333f882d1.title: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

e-5182.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
e-5182.problem:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th row, write the following determinant as a combination of $3 \times 3$ determinants:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081343/assets/502b9464378fb5030a72918f45938184f120773e4639f3f50f071ca82fc307ce.png)
e-5182.worked_solution:
Using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}10 & 2 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 7 & 9 \\ -2 & 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -6 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| & =(-6)\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+1\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-6)\cdot (-1)^{4+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 7 & 9 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{4+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}10 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 7 \\ -2 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =6\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 7 & 9 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}10 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 7 \\ -2 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081343/assets/a1c11cfd7d1cacae0881118776eb6b38dea7b92c4f542e8158e31bbfa59274ec.png)

e-4418.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
e-4418.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{4+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3 \times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-8)+(0-0) \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

decision.explanation: Expand along the third row (0,-5,-5,0). The cofactor signs in columns 2 and 3 are − and +, respectively, so the coefficients are (-5)(-1)=5 and (-5)(1)=-5. This gives option e.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
content.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expanding along the third row leaves only the entry 2 in column 4. Its cofactor sign is (-1)^{3+4}=-1, so the determinant equals -2 times the minor formed by deleting row 3 and column 4. Thus option c is correct.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
content.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expand along row 3, whose only nonzero entry is 3 in column 2. Its cofactor sign is (-1)^{3+2}=-1. Deleting row 3 and column 2 gives the minor in option e, with coefficient -3.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
content.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expand along row 4, (0,-2,1,0). The cofactor signs in columns 2 and 3 are + and −, giving coefficients -2 and -1. Deleting the corresponding columns produces the two minors in option e.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{42}+1\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-1)^{4+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{4+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
content.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{42}+1\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-1)^{4+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{4+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expand along row 4. Its only nonzero entry is -2 in column 2, with cofactor sign (-1)^{4+2}=1. Deleting row 4 and column 2 gives the displayed minor, multiplied by -2, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 11 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & -2 & 6 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-1)^{4+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & 6 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & 6 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
content.worked_solution:
The $4$th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 11 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & -2 & 6 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 & 1 & 8 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{41}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-1)^{4+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & 6 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ -3 & 6 & 1 \\ -4 & 1 & 8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expanding along the first row gives 3(-1)^{1+3} times the determinant of [[1,2,-1],[0,1,0],[2,-1,3]]. Expanding that minor along its second row gives 1·(1·3-(-1)·2)=5. Thus the original determinant is 3·5=15.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+1\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 5=15.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row
content.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+1\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 5=15.
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & -0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0 \\ -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{21}+5\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|+5|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-3-0)+5(-6-4) \\  & =3-50 \\  & =-47\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second  $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+1\cdot {C}_{22}+5\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-5|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =(0-2)-5(-8-4) \\  & =-2+60 \\  & =58\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|=-47+58=11.
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+1\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-4)\cdot {C}_{22}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =(-4)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(2+3)+2(1+6) \\  & =-20+14 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.
$$

\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -7 & 4 \\ -2 & 5 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| & =-2\cdot {C}_{41}+5\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =-2\cdot (-1)^{4+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{4+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}|+5\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}

Computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}| & =(-1)\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-4-7)-(-8+2) \\  & =11+6 \\  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second  $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-4-7)-(0+0) \\  & =-11-0 \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

  

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & -7 & 4 \\ -2 & 5 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=2(17)+5(-11)=-21.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -7 & 4\end{aligned}| & =(-1)\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-4-7)-(-8+2) \\  & =11+6 \\  & =17\end{aligned}
